title: The Information Pathways Hypothesis: Transformers are Dynamic Self-Ensembles

problem.claim: Dense self-attention creates many possible connectivity patterns, but pruning it during training is difficult because information pathways are dynamic and input-dependent.

gap.claim: Although few connectivity patterns contribute to or are essential for network performance, the abstract does not describe an existing training strategy that exploits the predictable overall distribution of dynamic information pathways.

contributions.claim: The authors hypothesize that transformers contain sparsely connected information pathways that can be trained independently.
The authors propose Stochastically Subsampled self-Attention, a training strategy intended to reduce self-attention memory and computational cost while also regularizing training.
The authors show that subsampled pathways can form an ensemble of sub-models within a network.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report reducing self-attention memory and computational cost by 4 to 8 times during training.
The authors report improved generalization over dense training.
The authors report experiments across NLP, computer vision, and graph learning tasks in generative and discriminative settings.

narrative_sequence.summary: Transformers use dense self-attention for flexible long-range connectivity, with exponentially many possible connectivity patterns across layers.
Few connectivity patterns contribute to performance, and dynamic input-dependent pathways make dense self-attention difficult to prune during training.
The authors hypothesize the existence of independently trainable, sparsely connected information pathways and note that their overall distribution is often predictable.
The authors propose Stochastically Subsampled self-Attention to reduce training cost and provide regularization.
The authors report that subsampled pathways can form effective ensembles and evaluate the method across multiple task domains and learning settings.

source_observation.claim: The overall distribution of dynamic information pathways is often predictable even when individual pathways depend on the input.

interpretation.claim: A system may obtain computational savings by sampling from predictable aggregate structure without deterministically pruning every input-dependent connection.

application.claim: For dynamic connectivity systems, investigate stochastic subsampling strategies that preserve aggregate pathway behavior during training.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that aggregate predictability is sufficient for every architecture, task, or input distribution.

source_observation.claim: Subsampled pathways can form an ensemble of sub-models that the authors report performs better than dense attention.

interpretation.claim: Stochastic structural variation during computation may provide both efficiency benefits and an ensemble-like generalization effect.

application.claim: When designing efficient neural systems, evaluate whether structured subsampling can serve simultaneously as approximation and regularization.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify which tasks, models, or sampling regimes are necessary for the reported advantage.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the SSA sampling algorithm or training procedure.
The abstract does not provide task-level datasets, baselines, sample sizes, or detailed results.
The abstract does not establish independent verification, reproducibility, or proof correctness.
